passages.title: Task 1
passages.text:
(1) When Tuya was ten, her school started a small vegetable garden behind the sports hall. At first she thought it was boring. She had to water the plants before lessons and pull out weeds after school while her friends played outside. But by the end of the summer she had grown her own carrots and potatoes, and she was surprised by how proud she felt.

(2) Tuya's teacher, Mrs Oyun, believes that school gardens teach much more than biology. "When children grow food themselves, they understand where it comes from, and they are far more willing to taste new vegetables," she says. "They also learn to be patient, because a garden never hurries."

(3) To see whether the garden was making any difference, the school asked parents to keep a simple diary of what their children ate at home. Teachers then compared the diaries written in the spring, before the garden opened, with those written in the autumn.

(4) The difference was surprisingly clear. In the autumn diaries, children ate vegetables more often, and many asked their parents to cook dishes they had tried at school. Several families even started small gardens of their own on their balconies.

(5) Of course, a garden is not a magic answer to every problem. It needs time, water and someone to look after it during the long summer holidays. Still, Mrs Oyun is sure that it is worth the effort. As she likes to tell her pupils, "Anyone can buy a tomato, but you will never forget the first one you grew."
